retrieved.text: It should be deafening, because there's exactly one other quantity in all of physics, famous for only ever going up, and that's entropy, the second law of thermodynamics. Entropy, loosely, is a measure of disorder, of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with what you see, and the second law says the total entropy of a closed system never decreases. So here you have two never-decreases laws sitting side by side, horizon area on one hand, entropy on the other, and a graduate student named Jacob Bekenstein looked at that parallel and did something bold. He said, maybe that's not a coincidence. Maybe the area of a black hole's horizon literally is a kind of entropy. That feels like a leap from, these two things behave similarly, to, they are the same thing. Why did he need to make it? Why not just admire the resemblance? Because without it, black holes let you break the second law, and that's intolerable.

retrieved.text: It doesn't prove the gravitational case beyond all doubt, because the analogy has limits, but it directly tests the mechanism, that a horizon plus a quantum, or even just a wavy, vacuum, makes thermal radiation. Now, with the glow established, let's collect the prize that started this whole thing, because Bekenstein turns out to be vindicated in the most complete way. Right, we started with Bekenstein saying area is entropy, and Hawking trying to knock it down. How does it end? It ends with Bekenstein not just rescued, but made exact. Once you know the black hole's temperature, thermodynamics lets you compute its entropy precisely, and the answer is stunningly clean. A black hole's entropy is one quarter of its horizon area, measured in natural quantum gravity units. Let me unpack natural units. There's a fundamental, smallest-ish length in physics, the Planck length, built out of the constants of gravity, quantum mechanics and the speed of light. It's the scale where gravity and quantum theory both matter at once, and it is fantastically tiny.

retrieved.text: Because without it, black holes let you break the second law, and that's intolerable. Here's the thought experiment that forced his hand. The second law is supposed to be sacred. The entropy of the universe always goes up. Now, take a cup of hot gas, which has a lot of entropy, a lot of disorder, and toss it into a black hole. It's gone. It crossed the horizon. You can never see it again. So the entropy you threw in has vanished from the outside universe. If the black hole itself has no entropy, then the total entropy of everything outside just went down. You'd have a perfect entropy disposal machine, feed the universe's disorder into black holes and the books look cleaner and cleaner. The second law would be a joke, you could violate it any afternoon. Unless the black hole's own entropy went up by at least as much as you threw in. Exactly the escape. Bekenstein says, When you drop that hot gas in, the black hole's mass increases a little, so its horizon area increases a little, and if area is entropy, the hole's entropy goes up by at least as much as the entropy you lost.

retrieved.text: So here's our plan for the hour. First we build the classical black hole, the one general relativity gives you, and I'll convince you it really is perfectly black and eternal. Then we bring in a puzzle from Thermodynamics, Bekenstein's puzzle, that says a black hole ought to have entropy, which sounds harmless until you realize it forces the hole to have a temperature. Then Hawking, trying to prove that idea wrong, brings in the quantum vacuum, and out falls radiation, a perfect thermal glow. And once we have the glow, everything cascades. Black holes evaporate, they have a genuine thermodynamics, and they hand us a paradox about information that is still open half a century later. Two ingredients, a horizon and the quantum vacuum, and the blackest object in the sky turns grey and mortal. Let's build the classical black hole first then. What actually is it? Strip down.

The densest possible in fact There a limit the Bekenstein bound that says a region of a given size can hold only so much entropy before it collapses into a black hole and the black hole is the object that saturates that limit exactly It is the maximally packed hard drive that physics permits And that really the deepest reason the area not volume fact matters The most information you can cram into any region is set by the area of its boundary not the volume inside Which brings us to what that did to physics So this one paper doesn't just make black holes glow, it reorganises how people think space and information relate. It does, and there's a neat closing of the circle in the pure thermodynamics too. Before Hawking, people had noticed that the mathematical laws governing black holes looked eerily like the laws of thermodynamics. There were four of them, matching up one for one.

retrieved.text: And anything with a non-zero temperature radiates. A hot poker glows red. Your own body glows in the infrared. Everything with a temperature above absolute zero gives off thermal radiation. So Bekenstein's idea, taken seriously, demands that a black hole radiate, and that is flatly, obviously impossible in general relativity, because we just spent ten minutes establishing that nothing gets out. So Hawking's reaction was, reasonably, this shows Bekenstein has gone too far, the temperature of a black hole must really be zero, the entropy business is just a suggestive analogy, and I'll do the calculation that proves it. So the paper we're celebrating was born as an attempt to debunk the very thing it ended up confirming. That's the shape of it. He set out to show black holes don't radiate, and the mathematics dragged him, apparently against his expectations, to the conclusion that they do. And the reason the calculation surprised him is that to do it properly, you can't stay inside general relativity.

response:
Bekenstein argued that a black hole must carry entropy because otherwise the second law of thermodynamics would be violated. He imagined dropping a hot, high‑entropy gas into a black hole. The gas’s entropy disappears from the observable universe, yet the black hole itself would have no entropy to compensate, so the total entropy would decrease—an impossible “entropy disposal machine.” To keep the second law intact, the black hole’s horizon area must increase by at least as much as the lost entropy, implying that the area itself is a measure of entropy [E2 @ 5:25-6:39].  

In addition, Bekenstein noted that the area of a black hole’s horizon sets a maximum amount of information that can fit inside a given region before it collapses. This “Bekenstein bound” shows that the most information‑dense object is a black hole, reinforcing the idea that its area is directly linked to entropy [E2 @ 4:26-5:30].
